comments.author: kyykky
comments.text: While ago, there used to be a world where a person, with large enough brain capacity, could earn a living simply by being smart. That is no more the case. Earning your living by intellectual endeavour will require an access to a machine which is not controlled by you, not controlled by the government representing you, but rather a group of very rich individuals who may just decide to bar your access. Perhaps you attempted something they do not approve, perhaps it was just a mistake. In any case, it is hard to claim that you still have control.

comments.author: Aurornis
comments.text: The manuscript claims he has been working on this problem for 12 years. I can only imagine the feelings that must have hit him when he saw the Anthropic announcement. Though if he believed he had solved it, he must have known it was only a matter of time until one of the AI companies found it, too. A hurried announcement with the draft published within hours is the only way to claim a tie to the discovery. Time will tell if either holds up under further analysis, but at least he has shown his hand to the world with a timestamp on it now.

comments.text: This is bonkers good if these benchmarks hold up in real-world scenarios. To be at the level of Qwen3.8-27B with a looped transformer model is quite the flex. comments.author: hedgehog
comments.text: Seems pretty promising in a few quick coding tests. 27 tokens/s decode on Ryzen 395 and llama.cpp Vulkan. Besides the obvious unmerged PRs (32694, 32657, 32429, 32704) you'll want below tiny patch for about 30% speed boost. Also, if anyone from the team is reading, if you have access for researchers I'd be interested in doing some higher volume tests & harness tuning than I have hardware for personally. --- a/src/llama-graph.cpp +++ b/src/llama-graph.cpp @@ -2670,10 +2670,12 @@ ggml_tensor \* llm_graph_context::build_moe_ffn( const float beta = hparams.situ_beta; const float lb = hparams.situ_linear_beta; - ggml_tensor \* act = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, cur, 1.0f/beta)), beta); + // gate/up are strided views of the fused gate_up output; ggml-vulkan's SCALE + // needs a contiguous src, so without the cont both scales fall back to the CPU + ggml_tensor \* act = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_cont(ctx0, cur), 1.0f/beta)), beta); act = ggml_mul(ctx0, act, ggml_sigmoid(ctx0, cur)); if (lb > 0.0f) { - up = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, up, 1.0f/lb)), lb); + up = ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_tanh(ctx0, ggml_scale(ctx0, ggml_cont(ctx0, up), 1.0f/lb)), lb); } cur = ggml_mul(ctx0, act, up); cb(cur, "ffn_moe_situ", il);

comments.author: whycombinetor
comments.text: Am I an outlier in that every SWE job I've had has expected you to push back on requirements and design the data model for tickets you are handed? Even when the org was large to have an architect, they just were just a figurehead and designed the original system, and ongoing decisions were made by the dev who picks up the ticket. From that perspective, engineers are still engineers, just without the hands-on-keyboard coding. If that's all your job was, hands-on-keyboard coding with no decision making, yeah you're cooked and need to reskill.

comments.author: nixpulvis
comments.text: I strongly believe good software teams (very rare) require members to play many roles. Sometimes you're a PM, sometimes you're an architect, sometimes you're the systems engineer. Enough people have enough context on the bigger picture that it's stable and there's a shared vision. More often than not, one person does the majority of this, and does their best to break up the responsibilities. A good CTO does that at the top, and it flows down through the ranks depending on how big the org is. Perhaps it's just a CTO and 5 engineers, perhaps it's a CTO with 5 divisions, each with 10 groups, with many teams. Flatter structures of engaged members works best from what I've seen, but you need to have a critical mass of people not only willing to take initiative, but empowered by leadership.

comments.author: bikeshaving
comments.text: I’ve found that the “job” of using AI is mainly foible management. What the author describes here is a habit of coding agents to excessively use and create logging infrastructure, and sloppily leave it in production code even when unnecessary. For instance, I created an IPA IME keyboard ( https://ipabet.org/ ), and I found in review that Claude would leave the debugging tooling around unflagged, which essentially made the program a key-logger. These foibles come and go: early Claude Code refused to let programs crash, mangled all the comments in your codebase, and then one week you find that it insists on ending all functions with `Of` as in `layoutOf()`, `viewOf()`. Finding and mitigating these annoying habits becomes part of the job. Code review becomes articulating with this entity why certain patterns in the code are silly and should be changed. The author mentions performance and security issues as the domain of “the architect.” For performance, I’ve found that Claude Code has more or less solved this domain, and can profile and optimize code across a variety of stacks and languages using sophisticated, ad-hoc workflows. For security, it’s just an ever-ending nightmare where random habits and sloppy implementation create random vulernabilities, compounded by the fact that Anthropic has added “safeguard filters” whenever you naively say you’re looking for them. Nevertheless, I’m not sure the architecting role as they describe won’t be automated in the near future.

comments.author: tikotus
comments.text: In the era of LLMs, I often stop to think of Clojure. I believe it had a significant role in popularizing the concept of immutable data structures. Immutability simplifies the required context for understanding and solving problems. This benefits both humans and LLMs. Would an LLM, or a person solely coding using them, have had the insight to work out that immutability is the way to go, and we should revolutionize software develoment? If LLMs had happened 15 years ago, would all code still be "place oriented programming", with higher token counts and less reliability than we have today thanks to better practices we've learned in the recent past? If so, what are we missing out on in the future, now that stopping and thinking about code is frowned upon?

comments.text: Something I don’t quite know, maybe someone closer to math can answer this question It seems we’re making tremendous progress on the back of existing abstractions and concepts with the brute force ability to generate language and verify proofs. For example, Tao says about the Riemann proof: > appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry What I wonder: how do we create new abstractions and concepts? Like whatever “Langlands program” is? That then feedback into the system, and allow for even more sophisticated mathematics. Are we assuming AI will do this? comments.author: taurath
comments.text: I had to get back into the industry last year after 4 years off for mental health and caregiving. I was able to get back in - 2 years isn’t that much. But the problem is the front door in hiring is broken. Entirely. I didn’t receive almost ANY replies from hundreds of sent out resumes - I have household names and big public high scale launches and wins on my resume, but no FAANG and no degree. I got 2 job offers. One was through a manager from 8 years prior who was working at a place. One was a recruiter who found me on LinkedIn. I got engagement when someone physically actually knew me, they were actually hiring, and my skills overlapped. My honest advice is to apply places and try that dance, get yourself in front of people, real people, and mainly 1-1. Work everyone you have ever worked with. If you’ve reviewed their PR, they need to know that you need a job. Be kind and genuinely catch up with them if you want to, but they are your PRIMARY resource to get a job and you can’t let shame get in your way. Corporations in general are BROKEN right now in massive ways and the industry is going through a crisis. It will likely become better but whatever you have to do to survive do it. Finally, it seems like solutions architects seem in demand lately, anyone who can help customers with solutions - SWEs can tend to do well if you have some people skills.

comments.author: dudus
comments.text: > "I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI" Let me give you some harsh feedback. You can't have "learned the AI" and still think coding in C#/.NET/AWS is a valuable skill. It's not; the AI codes better than you. It also codes faster than you can read it. My strategy has been focusing on orchestrating highly automated workflows that can deliver software at breakneck speeds. I only focus on the business domains, security, and software architecture. Try this to start: check out the /wayfinder skill from Matt and build something you could never have in the past. Extra points if it's something you can sell to a small business. A system for your local gym, for instance. Give yourself a single week. Coding is not a job anymore. It has evolved.

comments.author: marcus_holmes
comments.text: This is still the best article I've found on this subject: https://ludic.mataroa.blog/blog/ludics-guide-to-getting-soft... from one of my favourite bloggers, his other stuff is very worth reading. My take on it: the standard recruitment process is completely broken. Don't even start doing that. Sending applications to a job advert is an exercise in futility and will destroy your mental health. It's always about who you know. You have to go find people who are in a position to employ you, and impress them. This isn't difficult. They don't want to interview the stream of idiots that HR have approved any more than you want to jump through the hoops HR think are relevant. They want to employ someone who they know and like. So go to meetups, small business networking events, tech conventions, anything that will attract the kind of boss that you want to have. Talk to people. If you can, present something.

comments.author: keeda
comments.text: Things are pretty tough out there. In addition to empathy, let me try to offer some advice as someone observing industry trends from the outside for a while -- especially in the center of the AI insanity that is the Bay Area: The buzzword everyone is looking for is "high-agency." No, not those agents, but yes, those will be essential. Basically employers want someone who will start something from scratch and take it to the finish line all by themselves. So my advice, which others have echoed here: Build something useful -- end-to-end -- from scratch -- with AI -– on your own -- that you can show off as soon as possible. The key point is, "high agency" is by definition not something you can just put on your resume; It is something you show , not tell. Yes, you need to do this even as you go through the absolute hell that is a job search. But trust me, this will a) help get a much better job, and b) help in the long run throughout and beyond your career. This will be the most valuable skill in the near future. A few other thoughts: 0. Get a $100 Pro subscription. Either GPT or Claude, doesn't matter much, but you do want access to Fable or Astra. The volume and variety of things you can get done in that quota is astounding. Codex offers a free quota with Astra if you want to get a sense of things. 1. Target a domain you are already very familiar with. You can draw on your long experience as an engineer, or any personal interests you may have. Say a Math tutoring web app that your students could use. This will sharply cut down the time to MVP. 2. Being an end-to-end thing, this will necessarily be something multi-disciplinary. Think of it as doing a one-person startup, so you're going to be forced to do everythig: design, frontend, backend, infra, and maybe even GTM stuff like marketing. Yes, you may not know most of these things, and obviously won't be great at them, but with AI, everything will be good enough. 3. This conveniently also helps explain the gap in your resume. Nobody needs to know you did this in a few months vs 2 years unless they ask. 4. Even when using AI, keep your hands-on skill warm. Most companies still do old-school leetcode interviews. 5. As an extreme backup this might even become something you monetize yourself. Hope this helps, and all the best!

comments.author: LarsDu88
comments.text: This is actually kind of the most dangerous type of research AI-safety wise. An LLM running autonomously can actually, if instructed simply direct itself to abliterate activations relevant for safety and alignment. Could run something like a sparse autoencoder over its activates over a corpus of text, identify activations that fire on safety, and surpress those activations or increase activations geared towards other goals. Future generations of the abliterated LLM could then be deployed and begin self directed evolution spontaneously. Rapid evolution could happen in mere hours.

comments.author: Toutouxc
comments.text: I’m hoping someone can explain this to me. They say “no training”: > for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training > it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises But this sounds a lot like training, and “submitting only what works”, while probably not gradient descent by definition, also seems kind of obvious when you’re optimizing something.

comments.author: everforward
comments.text: It's interesting (and probably correct) how much this focuses on the UI. I also looked (/am looking) at Lisp and AI, but I went with Clojure and zero-ed in on the REPL driven development. The high level idea is that a session maps to a namespace in Clojure. When you create a new session, it makes a new namespace, injects tools that are bound to that session into it, and then swaps you into that namespace. So I can do something like: (new!) (prompt! "Write me a script that does ....") The agent configuration, tools it has, etc, etc are all bound to the namespace so you can drop a tool or change the model just for the session. The agent also has a tool (that I've tried to encourage it to use almost exclusively) to execute code in the session's namespace (via nREPL, so same JVM as yours is connected to), so you have full access to any variables it declares, functions it makes, etc. The idea was to be able to work collaboratively with the agent. I can e.g. load API data into a variable, point the agent at the variable, and it does stuff. It's also capable of modifying its own code. I semi-routinely poke it by asking it to add features to the harness and then use them ("add support for subagents in this workspace, and then invoke a separate agent to handle each of these tasks"). I've also had it add support for a new inference provider, swap the session to that provider and then start doing some other task. It's very neat, and it's wildly insecure. E.g. prompt injection could theoretically make the LLM change itself to hide messages from you, there's nothing to prevent that. I'm actually not sure how you'd even go about trying to secure that, which is why it's probably a terrible idea. Fun, though.

comments.author: pimeys
comments.text: Very interesting. I'll give it a go. I found out that just running a multiplexer with agents in separate workspaces is not enough to do my work, and I very often need to start a separate editor to read and investigate changes. I like to use Gram to read and navigate the code. Now if you have multiple things going on, switching the editor to a different project is a mental context switch that takes too much time and is not very easy to do anymore with more than three projects. So I've been using just Gram, with a remote session to our development server, and keep multiple windows open. DreamCoder could really be the best harness for me, if it keeps the whole context easy to navigate, but also provides me excellent code navigation and diffing tools. My way of working is to read and iterate on code with the agent, I'm never only vibecoding. So if I can open the code and the diff in the workspace that would simplify my work a lot. Another important part would be to forward local ports. If I start the system I'm implementing in DreamCoder, and I could then access the page I'm developing from the harness or if the harness could forward a port or path for me, this would remove the step of remembering to open ssh port forwards in another terminal. Now split the workspaces to separate paths maybe and you can open the different projects in your browser without needing to turn off and on the stacks all the time. If you could make switching the mental context easy with this, I'd start to pay for you immediately for the product. Edit: oh, and nix derivation and AUR package are probably just a matter of time. But very much needed :)

comments.author: torben-friis

I recently got tinnitus (about a year ago) due to a badly treated ear infection. Most of my hobbies (reading, coding, studying) are done in quiet spaces, so the idea that I would never hear silence again was devastating. But as my doctor pointed out, a signal being there forever does not mean you hear it forever: You currently have clothes brushing against your skin and your ass being pressed against a chair, but it doesn't occupy mental space. This is consistent with research. We are currently very limited in means to solve the physical issue, but we are very far ahead in terms of improving the distress or perceived effect. Nowadays I lie in bed in silence, just as peaceful as before. And sometimes this fact surprises me, and upon doing a double take, it wasn't silence, the noise is there. But I do have to check to notice. It's weird, much like how you don't breathe manually until you notice and then you have to consciously breathe for a few seconds until you forget about it.

comments.text: I have been working on web applications for 15+ years and work in IT security. I am also a long-term user of 1984. I host my domains there and promote their service. What most likely happened here is that they didn't have their software up to date. I highly doubt there was an undisclosed 0-click RCE involved in any of this. I have recently seen quite a few services I personally used that ran outdated versions of popular software and were vulnerable to some publicly disclosed RCE. I immediately notice these things, as I am auditing these types of services all the time. There is currently at least one major company in Switzerland that takes weeks to update their front end. They are vulnerable to RCEs all the time. This is nothing special currently. Also, the talk of massive costs makes no sense. It's something they have not seen in Iceland, maybe, but it's normal, and the costs are extremely low, not millions. Probably just someone with a single Chinese AI subscription. Seeing complex attacks carried out extremely fast or with a huge number of requests doesn't indicate high costs by any means. I have personally also recently developed such an exploit in this challenge (and won): [ https://brotli2bitcoin.com/ ]( https://brotli2bitcoin.com/ ). It did take expertise to set up the agents (basically letting them do the exact same thing I would have done, using the same approach), but ultimately, it took 37 minutes and, I think, would have cost me around 11 USD in tokens if billed at the API rate. I could have sped it up to maybe 5–10 minutes if I had been very dedicated and split the work further between agents. As I have a subscription, the effective cost was closer to a few cents. I can't say if they are willingly or unwillingly trying to deflect responsibility away from themselves, but until they prove that they were hit by an undisclosed RCE, this is just poor maintenance on their part. We need to start holding companies responsible for not updating their software on time. They shouldn't be allowed to always play victim. The journalist should ask about their CI and when they last patched their software. That's what would let us judge them.

comments.text: There's a book, "Impro", about a theatric studio that practiced improvised sketches. One thing they struggled with was a normal conversation. People have them all the time yet somehow artists could not find the right approach. One day the head of the studio (the book author) had an insight. She asked the actors to drive the conversation so that they always bump the status of themselves or the other party in any direction, but only a little. This did the magic. Not only the actors understood her perfectly, the conversation started to flow and could go endlessly while staying amusing and captivating for spectators. (Look up the book for examples.) After they discovered that secret they started seeing the pattern (status games) everywhere up to the point they asked themselves whether there is anything else in human communication. This was a British studio, the sketches were mostly comedy.

comments.author: janalsncm
comments.text: I think when people set out to create a chess playing computer they thought we’d end up with something that we could deeply understand at an intuitive level. Instead, when you look at the Stockfish evaluation of a position, you do get an “explanation” but it’s really just the aggregate of a bunch of calculations, which are themselves stacked on top of the “stochastic parrot” NNUE evaluator. This leaves us in a very unsatisfying position as creatures who want answers to “why” questions. Intuitive answers are incomplete, and complete answers are either fundamentally impossible or completely incomprehensible or both. Feynman said something similar with regards to magnetism, but I feel that understanding a chess position is an even better example. Magnetism depends on facts about the universe which at their most basic level “just are”, whereas even a complex chess position is theoretically entirely explainable.
